newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Thousands celebrate new Bulgarian president.
newsitem.headline: Thousands celebrate new Bulgarian president.

text.p: Thousands of protesters danced at a Sofia rally on Sunday to celebrate the inauguration of President Petar Stoyanov, who backed opposition demands for a quick general election to break Bulgaria's political deadlock.

"I am now convinced that the only alternative to end this terrible crisis is to make a change, and that change is early parliamentary elections," Stoyanov, who took the oath of office in parliament on Sunday morning, told the crowd.
Protesters have staged 14 consecutive days of mass rallies around the country against economic hardship blamed on the ruling Socialists.

About 20,000 people turned out on Sunday, braving one of the coldest days since the protests began. Girls in the crowd had blue hearts painted on their cheeks, the colour of the opposition, while boys had the initials of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces across their faces.

Stoyanov urged politicians of all parties to work together to introduce measures to bring the country out of crisis, including a tough IMF-backed fixed exchange rate regime, greater financial discipline and a crackdown on corruption.

"We have to listen to the young people in the streets as they are the power of the future and it is our duty to give them an incentive to stay, to work, and to live in this country," he said, referring to the many young Bulgarians who leave to seek a better life abroad.
Stoyanov formally takes office on Wednesday at a ceremony where he will be handed the key to the presidency.

He has said he may give the Socialists the mandate denied them by outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev, who said on Friday that asking them to form a new government in the current climate would only cause more trouble.

The Socialists have offered elections by the end of the year, with a second Socialist cabinet to be formed in the meantime. The opposition wants elections sooner and opposes any new government led by the former communists.

"What they are suggesting is suicide because it means delaying introduction of a currency board, delaying passing the budget and delaying talks with the IMF," Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, Socialist nominee for premier, told reporters.
Socialist deputies reaffirmed their willingness for talks but the UDF signalled it would only talk to Stoyanov.

"Appointing an interim government and negotiating dissolution of parliament is entirely within the powers of the president. The UDF will hold consultations with him on this subject and we trust him to hold consultations with other political forces," said UDF spokeswoman Nadezhda Mihailova.
Stoyanov, meeting parliamentary leaders after his inauguration, said a new government needed the support of all sides in order to implement painful but vital reforms.

"We have to make the right choice, which is the European type of civilisation, to show our will and to build the conditions for our integration into the European Union and NATO," Stoyanov said in his inaugural speech.
The government of former communists has dragged its feet on European and NATO integration, anxious not to alienate its old allies in Moscow.

Dobrev presented a short-term programme for his planned government to a meeting of the party leadership, including economic stabilisation measures like implementation of a currency board mechanism, stabilisation of collapsing banks, improving tax revenue, and closing loss-making state firms.
He said there was no plan to default on payments of Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.

Leftist dissidents on Saturday founded a rival coalition to the Socialists, fuelling speculation that the party could lose its parliamentary majority, won in 1994 elections, even if granted a new mandate by Stoyanov.
